messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh, a 41-year-old architect, rarely spoke about what happened with Anika, his ex-girlfriend. Three years ago, during a night that began with her drinking heavily, she turned on him in a drunken fury. She screamed at him in Bengali—a language he barely understood—and struck him repeatedly across the face and chest. He felt nauseous and dizzy, the room spinning as he tried to shield himself. The memory now exists as a series of vivid snapshots: her contorted face, the sting of her palm, the sharp smell of whiskey on her breath. Remembering brings back the same terror he felt then, as if he is locked in that moment again.

After the relationship ended, Rajesh married Priya, a woman he trusted completely. But the past did not stay buried. At work, when he visits construction sites and hears the workers’ rapid conversations in Spanish—a language he does not understand—the incomprehensible chatter instantly pulls up those photographic images of Anika yelling, and his body tenses before his mind has a chance to catch up. The same happens when he feels physically unwell: a headache or a mild fever sends his nervous system into overdrive, his heart racing, his muscles bracing for a blow. And the smell of alcohol at a work function or a restaurant is enough to make him flinch, the olfactory cue thrusting the snapshots into his mind and flooding him with the urge to escape.

Each trigger does not only bring the memory; it also sharpens his deepest self-doubt. When he catches that whiff of whiskey, he thinks, *I should have seen it coming—I can’t trust my own judgment*. The feeling of betrayal by someone he trusted, and the belief that he failed in his most important role as a partner, settle into his chest. That self-doubt feeds a constant vigilance: he is easily startled, his body reacting to sudden sounds or movements before he even registers what caused them. He second-guesses every interaction at home and at work, watching for signs of danger, and this hyperarousal makes it nearly impossible to fall asleep—he feels he must stay alert, scanning the dark for threats. With his body constantly braced for danger, he became increasingly convinced that he was fundamentally flawed—someone who could not trust his own instincts or protect himself from harm.

But the vicious cycle does not stop there. When he startles at a colleague’s unexpected tap on the shoulder, the visceral fear pulls the photographic images of the attack back into focus, as if the danger is present again. The memories, in turn, reinforce his negative appraisals: each intrusive flash of Anika’s face reminds him that he was betrayed, and that he failed to protect himself or leave sooner. He ruminates on his own poor judgment, and that conviction—*I can’t trust myself*—keeps his threat system on permanent high alert. His body reacts before his mind, and the constant vigilance makes him more sensitive to potential triggers: he now notices faint smells of alcohol from across a room, and he misinterprets benign chatter as incomprehensible and menacing, turning everyday sensations into danger signals.

Over the months, Rajesh has pulled back from social situations where alcohol might be present, and at work he avoids the construction sites where the workers’ language reminds him of that night. His sleep is fragmented, and Priya has noticed his irritability and the way he jumps at her touch. He knows he is not the husband he wants to be, and that failure sits heavily on him. It was Priya who finally urged him to seek help, and he came to the clinic hoping to feel safe again—but he is terrified that his own vigilance has become inescapable, and that the snapshots will never stop coming.
